args.text: [lane-vole] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to a server that has moved or been retired, so services fail. (2) Slow recovery: if a site switches to a backup server during an outage, cached answers delay the switch. (3) Lingering bad data: a poisoned or mistaken answer stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting users for longer.

[lane-vole] Networks fail in ways that leave a sender unsure whether a request worked, so retrying is often the only safe choice. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

[lane-vole] (1) Larger keys: a UUIDv7 (universally unique identifier, version 7) takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a normal whole-number key, so indexes and any tables that refer to it grow bigger. (2) Leaked timing: the first part of the value is a timestamp, so anyone who sees an ID can tell roughly when the row was created, and IDs made within the same millisecond are only ordered if the software takes care to do so.

[lane-vole] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes the main data, so that after a crash it can replay or undo unfinished work and stay correct. It also makes writes quicker, because adding to the end of a log is cheaper than updating many places in the main files straight away.

[lane-vole] (1) Pinning the client version keeps the results comparable: if the client changes between runs, you cannot tell whether a speed difference comes from the system under test or from the client. (2) It makes the benchmark repeatable, so you or anyone else can rerun it later and get results that are fair to compare, since new client releases may change behaviour or speed.

[lane-vole] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the senders to slow down when the workers cannot keep up, for example by making them wait, pushing back with an error, or dropping new work. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make every item wait longer.

[lane-vole] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same job is installed on two servers, or in two places on one server, so both fire at the same moment; (2) a run takes longer than the gap between runs, so the next run starts while the last is still going. One guard is a lock, for example a lock file or a database lock, that makes a second copy exit at once if one is already running.

[lane-vole] A tombstone is a small marker that says "this item was deleted", kept in place of the item itself. In a replicated store, simply removing data would let a copy that missed the delete send the old data back to the others, so the marker is kept and spread to every copy, and is only cleaned away after all copies have seen it.

[lane-vole] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs; (2) it fails only sometimes, often tied to timing, run order, or shared state, and a simple re-run makes it pass. A truly failing test fails the same way every time.

[lane-vole] A lease-based lock lets one worker hold a lock until a set expiry time. Clock skew means two machines disagree about the current time. (1) If the holder's clock runs slow, it thinks its lease is still valid after the lock service has already expired it and given it to another worker. (2) If the lock service's clock runs fast, leases end early. Either way, two workers may act as the owner at once, so the lock no longer protects the shared resource.
